content.title: Appointments and supply
content.text: Arrange blood tests, transport, medicine supply and interpreter or carer support. Check who reviews results and how you receive the decision before the next dose.

content.title: Paper copies and contacts
content.text: Keep the full handbook, three-page summary and wallet card together. The QR code is optional. Ask the team to replace every labelled example contact with your real oncology and out-of-hours details; ask for a new printed plan when treatment changes.

content.title: Your diagnosis and stage
content.text: Keep the pathology report, original melanoma site, stage and known sites of spread. This guide concerns advanced disease that cannot be removed completely by surgery or has spread; it does not describe a postoperative recurrence-prevention course.

content.title: The tumour test
content.text: A BRAF V600 test helps identify whether BRAF-targeted medicines are an option. A tumour mutation does not by itself mean an inherited family condition. Keep the exact result and ask how it changes your choices.

content.title: Scans and local treatments
content.text: Record the scans used to follow known disease. Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role for a particular site; ask for their timing and risks to be added to the overall plan.

content.title: New changes still matter
content.text: Report a new lump, changing mole, persistent skin sore or unexplained symptom. A response at one site does not establish that every other symptom is harmless.

content.title: Practical arrangements
content.text: Know where and when bloods are taken, how results reach the prescriber, and how to obtain the next supply or appointment. Ask for written instructions in a format you can use without a phone.

content.title: When life is affected
content.text: Tell the team about fatigue, pain, appetite, sleep, mood and ability to work or care for others. Practical and supportive care can accompany anticancer treatment; you do not have to wait until treatment ends.

content.title: Food, fluids and activity
content.text: Keep meals and fluids manageable and follow any individual fluid or diet restrictions. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to how you feel. Ask for dietetic or rehabilitation help if intake, weight, strength or mobility is falling.

content.title: Sexual health
content.text: Tell the team about sexual symptoms, relationship concerns or practical difficulties with the agreed precautions. Ask for a private discussion and specialist support when needed.

content.title: Support alongside treatment
content.text: Ask about symptom control, psychological support, finances, transport, work and help at home. Palliative or supportive care can be used alongside anticancer treatment to improve comfort and function.

content.title: A person you trust
content.text: If helpful, bring a family member or supporter and agree what information may be shared. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information when needed; use teach-back to check the schedule and urgent plan.

content.title: Your document set
content.text: Keep consent information, the three-page summary, complete handbook, treatment card, test plan and real contact details together. The QR opens more information but essential instructions remain available in print.

content.title: A treatment summary
content.text: Record medicines and doses received, important side effects, admissions, last-dose date, ongoing symptom treatment and the clinician responsible for follow-up. Ask for an updated paper copy for your GP and other treating teams.

content.title: Your next review
content.text: Confirm the next blood test, scan and review, who explains the result, and which symptoms should trigger contact sooner. Keep actual daytime and out-of-hours numbers accessible after treatment stops.

content.name: Vismodegib
content.explanation: Vismodegib blocks a protein called Smoothened in the Hedgehog signalling pathway. This pathway can drive basal cell cancer growth. Blocking it can also affect normal hair follicles, taste and muscle function, which helps explain hair loss, altered taste and cramps. This treatment is different from a cream applied to a skin lesion.
content.watch: Keep four-week blood tests and the pregnancy-prevention programme. Report cramps, loss of strength, reduced intake, weight loss and severe skin symptoms.
risks: Altered or lost taste and poor appetite
Severe harm to pregnancy; prolonged prevention requirements

content.title: Eating, activity and practical help
content.text: Report falling intake, weight loss, pain or fatigue early. The team can tailor nutrition, activity, wound, psychological and practical support to your needs.

content.title: Required safety checks and your individual disease-assessment plan

rows.label: Bloods and organ safety
cells: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests; medicine review and pregnancy-prevention programme assessment for women and men. If pregnancy is possible, a supervised pregnancy test is needed within seven days before starting.

Full blood count, kidney and liver tests every four weeks. Review cramps, strength, taste, eating, weight, hair/skin changes and treatment tolerance. Pregnancy testing is monthly when applicable, even if periods stop.
Contact the team for new symptoms; extra tests may be needed between scheduled checks.
Safety bloods do not by themselves show whether cancer is responding.

Agree continuing clinical/skin review, any response imaging and support for ongoing effects. The pregnancy-prevention, donation and breastfeeding restrictions continue after the last dose for their specified periods.

rows.label: Cancer, skin and daily function
cells: Record diagnosis, stage, current disease sites and the baseline assessment.
Keep the source-specific skin and clinical reviews and the individually agreed response assessments.
Record new lesions, lumps, wound changes, pain and effects on usual activities.
Write the next examination or scan date and the responsible team; no universal scan or tumour-marker interval is assumed.

Keep follow-up for the treated lesion and for other skin cancers. Examination and any imaging are tailored to the disease and treatment; locally advanced disease needs an individual plan. Continuing precautions after vismodegib are part of follow-up even when the cancer medicine has stopped.

rows.label: Medicines and continuing precautions
cells: Review all medicines and the pregnancy/fertility plan.
Review treatment taken or received, holds, adverse effects and supportive medicines.
Keep the actual urgent contacts and do not restart a held medicine yourself.
Bring the medicine list and treatment summary to other services.

Vismodegib can cause severe harm to an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant need the formal pregnancy-prevention programme, including two recommended contraceptive methods (one highly effective method plus a barrier method), unless the agreed alternative is continuous abstinence, during treatment and for 24 months after stopping. Pregnancy tests are supervised before treatment and monthly, even with absent periods. Men must use a condom, with spermicide if available, during sex with a female partner during treatment and for two months afterwards, including after a vasectomy. Report a suspected patient or partner pregnancy immediately. Do not breastfeed or donate blood during treatment or for 24 months afterwards; do not donate semen during treatment or for two months afterwards. Ask the team to explain and document the full programme; this summary does not replace its materials.

content.note: The team supplies actual dates and resolves any source ambiguity. A reference period does not replace a prescription, a local monitoring plan or an individual treatment decision.

content.title: Appointments and supply
content.text: Arrange dates, medicine supply, transport and any needed interpreter or carer support. Ask whether bloods are taken in the oncology unit or elsewhere and how the result reaches the prescriber.

content.title: Paper copies and contact information
content.text: Keep this complete handbook, the three-page summary and the wallet card together. The QR code is optional. Ask the team to add your actual contacts and print a revised plan when treatment changes.

content.title: Confirm the diagnosis and extent
content.text: Keep the biopsy result, original site, dates and details of previous treatment. Basal cell carcinoma usually remains local, but some tumours become difficult to remove or rarely spread. Your team should explain whether the present problem is locally advanced disease or metastatic disease.

content.title: Why tablets are being considered
content.text: The cited NCCP vismodegib pathway concerns symptomatic metastatic BCC, or locally advanced BCC unsuitable for surgery or radiotherapy. Ask what makes those local treatments unsuitable in your case and what benefit is realistic. A systemic capsule is different from a cream for a small superficial lesion.

content.title: Record earlier local treatment
content.text: Record operations, margin results, reconstruction, radiotherapy and any previous BCC medicines. The effect on sight, movement, pain, wound healing and appearance may influence choices. More than one specialist may be needed to agree the sequence and practical support.

content.title: Inherited conditions and multiple cancers
content.text: Tell the team if you have had many BCCs at a young age or an established inherited condition such as Gorlin syndrome. This does not mean everyone with BCC needs genetic testing. Ask whether a specialist skin-surveillance or genetic advice plan is appropriate for your own history.

content.title: A visible lesion is only one part of assessment
content.text: Changes in a lesion, pain or a wound may be useful to track, but they do not replace examination and any agreed imaging. Report new skin lesions separately. If you use photographs, agree how and when the clinical team will compare them and how you will keep them private.

content.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
content.text: Record surgery, radiotherapy and other anticancer medicines separately, including dates and the specialist responsible. This schedule does not automatically include or authorise another treatment. Ask whether any overlap changes tests, symptoms to report or the timing of appointments.

content.title: Practical preparation
content.text: Arrange medicine supply, transport, interpreter or carer support before it is needed. Bring the alert card, symptom record and questions. Ask which appointments require someone to accompany you and how to obtain urgent advice outside normal hours.

content.title: Getting the result
content.text: For each test, record its purpose, due date, result and action. Agree how results reach you and who checks a result from another hospital. If an appointment or result has not arrived, contact the named service rather than assuming no news means no action is needed.

content.title: Eating, drinking and activity
content.text: Tell the team early about nausea, taste change, a sore mouth, diarrhoea or falling weight. Ask for an individual fluid and food plan if heart, kidney or other conditions limit intake. Gentle activity and planned rest can help maintain function; adjust to symptoms and ask for support when fatigue limits daily life.

content.title: Protect your skin
content.text: Use shade, protective clothing, a hat and broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, and avoid tanning beds. Reapply sunscreen according to its instructions. Protection matters even when it is cloudy; choose a practical approach that lets you remain active safely.

content.title: Know the pattern of your skin
content.text: Ask how to examine your skin, scars and relevant lymph-node areas and how often your own team recommends doing so. A mirror or a trusted helper can make hard-to-see areas easier to check. Report a new or changing lesion, a non-healing sore or a new lump rather than waiting for a routine visit.

content.title: Photographs are optional
content.text: If useful, keep a dated photograph with consistent lighting and a size reference, following your team’s advice. Photographs are optional and do not diagnose a cancer or replace examination. Keep them privately; this printable passport does not require you to upload images or other personal health information.

content.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
content.text: Use the dressings and skin-care plan recommended for your lesion and treatment. Ask before applying new creams or remedies to an open or treated area. Worsening pain, discharge, redness, bleeding or loss of function needs advice; routine skin-care instructions are not a substitute for assessment.

content.title: Benefits and uncertainties
content.text: Ask what evidence applies to your diagnosis, stage, biomarker and treatment setting, what outcome the team hopes to improve, and what may happen without this treatment. A trial average cannot predict an individual result; a benefit measured in one setting should not be transferred to another.

content.title: Alternatives and review points
content.text: Discuss other suitable treatments, clinical trials if relevant, local treatment options and symptom-focused care. Ask when the decision will be reviewed and what would prompt a change. Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life alongside anticancer treatment.

content.title: Help with daily life
content.text: Tell the team about work, transport, caring responsibilities, cost concerns, body image, anxiety or sleep. Ask which nurse, social worker, dietitian, rehabilitation professional or support organisation can help. Use resources relevant to your country and service; a US guide may describe different access or funding.

content.title: Shared understanding
content.text: Ask someone on the team to check that you can explain the medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route in your own words. An interpreter, large-print copy or a trusted supporter can help; none requires you to use a smartphone.

content.title: Your follow-up plan
content.text: Keep follow-up for the treated lesion and for other skin cancers. Examination and any imaging are tailored to the disease and treatment; locally advanced disease needs an individual plan. Continuing precautions after vismodegib are part of follow-up even when the cancer medicine has stopped.

content.title: The complete paper version
content.text: This handbook can be used without a phone: keep the schedule, symptom advice, medicine list, tests and contacts together. The QR code is an optional route to the matching regimen information. Ask the team to print updates when your plan changes and keep the latest dated copy.

content.title: Where it started and where it is now
content.text: A neuroendocrine tumour (NET) starts in cells that receive signals and can release hormones. The original organ is the primary site. A pancreatic NET is different from the more common pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Stage describes how far the cancer has spread; the stage system depends on its original site. A tumour in the liver may be a NET that spread there from elsewhere.

content.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
content.text: Differentiation describes how the cells look under the microscope. Grade describes their growth activity. Ki-67 is a laboratory measure of the proportion of tumour cells showing a marker of cell growth and helps assess grade in relevant NETs. It is not the percentage of your body affected and is not a survival percentage. Ask for the exact pathology wording, grade and Ki-67 result, including the sample date.

content.title: Grade is different from stage
content.text: A low-grade NET can have spread, and a high-grade tumour is not automatically stage 4. Well-differentiated grade 3 NET and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are different diagnoses with different treatment choices. These medicine guides must not be applied to another diagnosis simply because its name contains neuroendocrine.

content.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
content.text: A functioning NET causes a hormone-related syndrome. A nonfunctioning NET does not cause a recognisable excess-hormone syndrome, but it can still grow or cause symptoms by its size or location. Ask which description applies to you. A positive somatostatin receptor scan does not by itself mean the tumour is functioning.

content.title: Your diagnosis record
content.text: Keep the primary site, differentiation, grade, Ki-67 if reported, stage or sites of spread, hormone syndrome and receptor-scan result together in your passport. Ask the team to explain changes rather than trying to interpret one result in isolation.

content.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
content.text: Blood counts measure infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests help the team assess how your body can handle treatment. The schedule for your medicine is shown separately. Attend these checks even when you feel well; a scan does not replace them.

content.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
content.text: CT and MRI help show tumour size and where it is. A somatostatin receptor (SSTR) scan looks for receptor targets that certain treatments can attach to. An FDG-PET scan answers a different question about tumour activity and may be useful in selected cases. You will not necessarily need every scan. The specialist decides which test can change your care.

content.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
content.text: The team may measure selected blood or urine markers when they answer a question about your NET or symptoms. These can include serotonin-related testing such as 5-HIAA for selected patients, or specific pancreatic hormones. Chromogranin A is not a universal test before every treatment. A changing marker alone does not prove cancer growth. Record why each test is being done, how to prepare and who will explain it.

content.title: Preparing for a test
content.text: Ask whether you need fasting, a timed urine collection, dietary preparation or a medicine review. Follow the laboratory’s instructions for your particular test. Do not stop an acid-suppressing medicine, diabetes medicine or hormone-control treatment yourself. Tell the team about kidney problems, allergies and all medicines before a scan or blood test.

content.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
content.text: A heart ultrasound may be needed for particular treatment risks or to assess heart-valve problems associated with a hormone syndrome. It is not required on the same timetable for every NET. Depending on the diagnosis, age and family history, the team may offer genetic counselling; some NETs occur with inherited conditions such as MEN1. A tumour gene test and an inherited-risk test are not interchangeable.

content.title: Who does what, and when?
content.text: Use the passport to write each test, its purpose, planned date, booking service, result-review contact and next step. Your consultant sets response-scan and marker intervals. The postoperative schedules in general guides are not automatically the right schedule while you are taking these medicines.

content.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
content.text: Record your usual bowel pattern, flushing, pain, appetite, weight and energy before starting. Note what changes, how long it lasts, what you were taking and how it affects daily life. This helps the team distinguish a hormone problem from treatment toxicity without assuming that every symptom is cancer progression.

content.title: Hormone-related symptoms
content.text: Depending on the tumour, excess hormones may cause flushing, frequent watery stools, wheezing, acid-related pain or blood-sugar disturbances. An insulin-producing tumour can cause low blood sugar. Not every NET causes these problems. Ask which symptoms matter for your diagnosis and whether you need a separate rescue plan.

content.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
content.text: Somatostatin analogue injections and other symptom treatments may continue alongside anticancer treatment when prescribed. They may have their own appointment dates. Never stop them simply because tablets are paused. PRRT requires a carefully coordinated interruption and restart plan, which the nuclear-medicine service must supply.

content.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
content.text: Tell the surgical, dental, anaesthetic or imaging team if you have a hormone-producing NET or a previous hormone crisis. Ask your specialist whether special preparation is needed. Carry your current medicines and emergency plan; the wallet card supports this information but does not replace specialist instructions.

content.title: What are we trying to achieve?
content.text: Ask whether the main aim is to slow growth, reduce tumour size, relieve hormone symptoms, make another treatment possible or protect day-to-day quality of life. The aim and likely benefit depend on your particular NET and previous treatment. A stable scan may represent useful control even without tumour shrinkage.

content.title: How treatments fit together
content.text: Some people need surgery, hormone-control treatment, tablets, chemotherapy, PRRT, liver-directed treatment or external radiotherapy at different points. These are not all automatically part of your regimen. Ask the multidisciplinary team to draw your own sequence and name the clinician coordinating it.

content.title: Choosing between options
content.text: Ask why this option suits your tumour site, grade, growth rate, symptoms, receptor status and other health conditions. Discuss alternatives, the option of observation when appropriate, supportive care, and any suitable clinical trial. A treatment listed in a US guide is not a guarantee of availability or funding in Ireland.

content.title: Evidence is about groups
content.text: A trial can measure time before cancer worsens, tumour shrinkage or survival. These are different outcomes. A group result does not predict your own response or lifespan. Ask how closely the study patients match your diagnosis and what benefit would make the treatment worthwhile to you.

content.title: Review points and shared decisions
content.text: Agree when you will review symptoms, tests and scans, and what would lead to continuing, delaying, changing or stopping treatment. Discuss work, caring duties, travel and the effects you most want to avoid. You can revisit your choices as your situation changes.

content.title: Food, weight and digestion
content.text: Tell the team about weight loss, poor appetite, early fullness, persistent diarrhoea or greasy stools. Ask for a dietitian familiar with NETs and your surgery or medicines. Different causes need different support; do not assume every bowel symptom needs the same diet or medicine. Ask whether digestive-enzyme assessment or replacement is relevant to you.

content.title: Fluids and safe activity
content.text: Follow your individual fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea, kidney disease or heart problems. Balance manageable activity with rest. Tell the team if fatigue, dizziness, pain or breathlessness limits usual tasks; these symptoms can have treatable causes.

content.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
content.text: Living with repeated tests and treatment can affect sleep, mood, relationships and confidence. Ask about psychological support, sexual health, fertility advice, symptom-control services and support for carers. Supportive or palliative care aims to improve comfort and daily life and can accompany active anticancer treatment.

content.title: Practical help
content.text: Ask your nurse or social worker about transport, work, finances, home support, caring responsibilities and local NET support organisations. A general resource list may include services in other countries; your team can identify options available to you.

content.title: A record that works without a phone
content.text: Keep the printed schedule, medicine list, tests, contact numbers and written emergency instructions together. The full handbook contains the information in sequence for offline reading. The QR code is an optional route to more information; it is not needed to call for help or follow your paper plan.

content.title: Questions to take to the next visit
content.text: What is my exact diagnosis and grade? What is treatment trying to achieve? Which tests are mandatory for this medicine, and which depend on my NET? Who reviews results? What symptoms mean call now? What support would help me live as well as possible?

content.name: Radiotherapy
content.alias: External-beam treatment planned by radiation oncology
content.type: Treatment focused on the brain tumour area
content.mechanism: Damages DNA in the treated area
content.explanation: Radiotherapy directs high-energy radiation at the tumour and a planned surrounding area. It aims to damage tumour-cell DNA while limiting dose to nearby healthy tissue. Fatigue, scalp irritation, hair loss and swelling can occur; longer-term effects depend on the treatment area and dose.
content.watch: Report new or worsening headache, vomiting, weakness, speech or memory change. The radiotherapy team gives a separate skin-care and symptom plan.
risks: Hair loss in the treated area
Possible delayed effects on thinking and function

content.title: Steroid and seizure plans
content.text: Keep steroids and seizure medicines on their own written schedules if prescribed. They are not routine medicines for every patient, and chemotherapy rest days do not automatically mean stopping them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions.

content.title: Safety tests, symptoms and response review

rows.label: Blood count / kidneys / liver
cells: FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose, HBsAg and anti-HBc
FBC weekly during six-week RT; kidneys/liver before week 4
Continue arranged checks and recovery review before adjuvant treatment
Day 1 FBC/renal/LFT each cycle; Day 22 FBC under EMA guidance
LFT after cycles; follow delayed toxicity after the last dose

rows.label: Neurology / medicines / function
cells: Record neurological symptoms, daily function and current medicines
Review seizures, headache, cognition, mood, walking and any steroid plan
Report changes early; do not wait for the next MRI
Review treatment tolerance, medication support and patient goals
Agree follow-up and rehabilitation or symptom support

rows.label: MRI / diagnosis
cells: Confirm integrated diagnosis, molecular results and baseline imaging
MRI timing according to the neuro-oncology plan
Keep the booking and result-review contact in your passport
Interpret scan with symptoms, treatment effects and clinical review
Agree the next imaging and clinical review

content.note: The team books and reviews each test. Mandatory medicine-safety checks are distinct from individually timed MRI and tumour-tissue tests. There is no universal blood tumour marker for these treatment cycles.

content.title: Help with the daily plan
content.text: Ask a trusted person to help check the calendar if memory, vision, fatigue or hand strength makes treatment difficult. Confirm who is responsible for checking doses, collecting medicine, transport and calling for help. Keep consent and personal preferences central.

content.title: What each part does
content.text: Temozolomide crosses into the brain and creates chemical changes in DNA. If the damage cannot be repaired, a cell may stop dividing or die. Healthy blood-forming cells can also be affected, which helps explain blood-count changes, infection and bleeding risks. Nausea prevention and liver monitoring are important too. Radiotherapy directs high-energy radiation at the tumour and a planned surrounding area. It aims to damage tumour-cell DNA while limiting dose to nearby healthy tissue. Fatigue, scalp irritation, hair loss and swelling can occur; longer-term effects depend on the treatment area and dose.

content.title: When to seek help
content.text: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Contact the team promptly for a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms that prevent drinking. Do not restart held chemotherapy without instructions.

content.title: Support medicines
content.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids. PJP-prevention medicine is required during temozolomide with radiotherapy in this NCCP regimen. Your team supplies the prescription and decides how long to continue, including if lymphocyte counts remain low. Do not stop it just because radiotherapy has finished. Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting. Keep steroids and seizure medicines on their own written schedules if prescribed. They are not routine medicines for every patient, and chemotherapy rest days do not automatically mean stopping them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions.

content.title: The name and location
content.text: Gliomas begin in supporting cells of the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different diagnoses. A tumour that spread to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and is not covered by these glioma regimens. Record the exact integrated diagnosis and where it is located.

content.title: Grade is not the same as stage
content.text: Grade describes features linked to how a tumour behaves. Adult gliomas are usually discussed by their type, grade and molecular findings rather than the stage system used for many other cancers. Grade 4 does not mean cancer has spread through the body. Ask your specialist to explain your own report and any older terminology in the treatment protocol.

content.title: IDH and 1p/19q
content.text: IDH1 or IDH2 changes and loss of parts of chromosomes 1p and 19q help classify particular gliomas. The combination of findings matters: one result should not be read in isolation. These tests are usually performed on tumour tissue. They do not automatically mean a change has been inherited or that relatives need testing.

content.title: MGMT promoter methylation
content.text: MGMT is involved in repairing certain DNA damage. Methylation of its promoter can reduce that repair activity and helps the team discuss the likely benefit of temozolomide in relevant settings. It is not a blood tumour marker, a percentage of tumour left, or an individual survival prediction. Record the reported result and ask how it affects your treatment choice.

content.title: A useful diagnosis record
content.text: Keep the biopsy or operation date, pathology wording, grade, IDH result, 1p/19q result and MGMT result if tested. Mark a result as pending or not applicable rather than assuming it is negative. Ask whether specialist pathology review or further testing would change the plan.

content.title: Safety blood tests
content.text: A full blood count checks infection-fighting white cells, oxygen-carrying red cells and platelets that help stop bleeding. Kidney and liver tests help assess treatment safety. Attend the regimen’s required tests even when you feel well; a reassuring scan does not replace them. The schedule in this guide separates checks before, during and after treatment.

content.title: MRI and neurological review
content.text: MRI is the main scan used to assess many gliomas. Your team also considers symptoms, strength, movement, speech, memory, daily function and medicines such as steroids. Tell staff before MRI about implants or metal, kidney problems, previous contrast reactions or difficulty lying still. Ask about support if scans make you anxious.

content.title: Changes on a scan need interpretation
content.text: After treatment, inflammation and other treatment effects can resemble tumour growth on MRI. This is sometimes called pseudoprogression. The team may need comparison scans, specialist imaging or further assessment before deciding what a change means. New or worsening symptoms still need prompt review; do not assume they are harmless treatment effects.

content.title: An individual follow-up timetable
content.text: Write the next MRI date, what question it should answer and who will explain the result. Timing depends on your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous findings. General follow-up intervals in an international booklet are not automatically your schedule. These regimens do not require a generic CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or a blood tumour marker before every cycle.

content.title: Keep results with decisions
content.text: Use the passport to distinguish a test being booked, completed and reviewed. Record the agreed next step and whom to call if an appointment or result is missing. Do not alter chemotherapy or steroids yourself in response to a number or scan report.

content.title: Know your usual symptoms
content.text: Write down your usual headache, strength, walking, speech, vision, memory, mood, sleep and seizure pattern before treatment. Note new changes, when they started and how they affect daily tasks. With your permission, a trusted person can help spot changes or record what happened.

content.title: Urgent neurological changes
content.text: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions.

content.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
content.text: Steroids may be prescribed to reduce swelling around the tumour. They are not automatically needed for everyone. Ask for the exact dose, time, review date and any taper plan. Do not stop or change them suddenly without advice. Report sleep or mood changes, increased thirst, infection symptoms or muscle weakness and ask which additional checks or protection you need.

content.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
content.text: If prescribed, take seizure medicines on the agreed schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and whom to contact for breakthrough symptoms. Some medicines can affect mood, alertness or interact with treatment. Do not start, stop or switch them yourself. A rescue medicine needs an individual plan and training for whoever may give it.

content.title: Safety at home and outside
content.text: Ask your clinical team about driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery in light of your symptoms and any seizures. Local medical and licensing rules need individual advice; this guide does not give a universal driving clearance date. Occupational therapy can help adapt daily routines and the home.

content.title: Understand the sequence
content.text: Surgery or biopsy, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and follow-up have different jobs. Ask your team to draw the intended sequence and identify where you are now. Concurrent treatment means treatments overlap; adjuvant treatment follows the main treatment. A change of phase may change the dose, blood tests and support medicines.

content.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
content.text: Ask whether the aim is to control the tumour, delay growth, relieve symptoms, preserve function or a combination of these. Discuss likely benefits, burdens, alternatives and what would prompt a pause or stop. The answer depends on the exact diagnosis, previous treatment and your priorities.

content.title: Put evidence in context
content.text: Clinical trials describe groups of people and may use older pathology names or different schedules. They cannot predict one person’s response or lifespan. Ask how closely the evidence matches your tumour and treatment. No benefit number from one schedule should automatically be applied to another.

content.title: Discuss options available to you
content.text: Ask about appropriate clinical trials, specialist opinions, symptom support and other treatment options. A medicine or device described in an international guide is not automatically licensed, funded or suitable in Ireland. The treating multidisciplinary team explains what is available and relevant.

content.title: Make room for your priorities
content.text: Bring up fatigue, thinking, independence, family time, work, travel and side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for information at a pace and in a format that suits you. You may ask for a trusted person to join the discussion, written notes and time to reconsider decisions.

content.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
content.text: Tell the team about word-finding, attention, memory, reading, vision or planning difficulties. Rehabilitation may include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, or neuropsychological support. Written routines, rest breaks and help with medicine organisation can make day-to-day care more manageable.

content.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
content.text: Report poor appetite, weight change, vomiting or constipation early. Ask for dietitian help if eating is difficult. Use the prescribed anti-sickness and bowel plan; do not wait until symptoms are severe. Choose activity that is safe for your balance and strength and balance it with rest. Ask about treatable causes of fatigue.

content.title: Emotional support and carers

content.title: Work, transport and finances
content.text: Ask the specialist nurse or social worker about getting to treatment, time off work, benefits, caring responsibilities and support at home. Plan who can help with daily capsules and appointments if your memory, vision or fatigue makes these difficult.

content.title: Supportive care and future wishes
content.text: Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life while active treatment continues. You can discuss future care preferences and who you want involved in decisions at a time that suits you. Ask the team for Irish advice and documentation rather than using legal or hospice rules from a US booklet.

content.title: Support medicines
content.text: Lomustine and procarbazine have moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Vincristine alone has minimal emetic risk. The team supplies a day-specific anti-sickness plan, including the procarbazine days, and a rescue plan. Vincristine can slow the bowel through its effect on nerves. Preventive laxatives are recommended in NCCP; follow the prescribed plan and report constipation early. Severe abdominal pain, vomiting or inability to pass stool or wind needs urgent advice. Procarbazine has important interactions. Avoid alcohol during treatment and follow the pharmacist’s written food restrictions and advice about when restrictions end. Check all prescription, over-the-counter, herbal and supplement products before taking them. Keep any prescribed seizure medicine and steroid plan separate from the PCV calendar. Report new weakness, tingling, gait change or constipation before vincristine. A medicine review is needed before adding any treatment for symptoms.

content.name: Dabrafenib
content.explanation: A BRAF V600 change can keep the cell-growth pathway switched on. Dabrafenib blocks the altered BRAF protein. It is paired with a MEK inhibitor to act on the same pathway at another point. The BRAF result comes from tumour testing; it does not automatically mean a hereditary condition.
content.watch: Fever needs the written hold/contact plan. Check other medicines and contraception because interactions can matter.
risks: Skin rash and new skin tumours

content.name: Trametinib
content.explanation: MEK carries growth signals further along the pathway below BRAF. Trametinib blocks MEK alongside dabrafenib. Normal heart, eye, lung and other tissues can also be affected, which is why scheduled tests and prompt symptom reporting matter.
content.watch: Attend cardiac tests. New eye symptoms, cough, breathlessness, swelling or severe diarrhoea need prompt review.
risks: Bleeding, liver changes and muscle injury

content.text: Keep the pathology summary, original skin site, stage and details of any lymph-node involvement together. content.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
content.text: Record what surgery removed and whether the present medicine is postoperative treatment to lower recurrence risk or treatment of cancer that remains or has spread. Radiotherapy, stereotactic treatment or another operation may have a separate role; their timing and side effects need their own plan.

content.title: Stage and response are different
content.text: Stage describes the extent of melanoma at diagnosis or a later reassessment. A response assessment asks how known cancer has changed with treatment. In the adjuvant setting there may be no visible tumour to measure: surveillance looks for recurrence while safety checks look for medicine effects.

content.title: A new skin change still needs review

content.name: Nivolumab
content.explanation: Nivolumab blocks PD-1, a signal that can reduce T-cell activity. This can help immune cells act against melanoma, but it can also allow inflammation in healthy organs. It is not conventional chemotherapy and side effects can occur even after doses have stopped.
content.watch: Carry your immunotherapy alert card and report new symptoms early, including after treatment ends.
risks: Immune inflammation of bowel, lungs, liver or kidneys
Thyroid, pituitary, adrenal and glucose problems
Skin reactions and rare severe skin injury
Rare heart, muscle, neurological and eye inflammation
Some immune effects need long-term treatment

content.name: Ipilimumab
content.explanation: Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, another checkpoint involved in controlling T cells. Combining it with nivolumab increases immune activity and can increase immune-related toxicity. The four-dose combination phase has a different treatment plan from nivolumab maintenance.
content.watch: New diarrhoea, abdominal pain, severe headache or unusual weakness needs early contact. Do not wait for the next infusion.
risks: Rare neurological, eye, heart or muscle inflammation
Immune effects during or after treatment
